- What the Chinese Youtube Taught me About Colour Theory: Kind: captions Language: en The truth is that all these things we've been taught about complimentary colors and analogous palettes are probably harming us more than they are helping us. Because after meticulously studying from the Chinese YouTuber Billy Billy, I've discovered that Chinese artists tend to approach color theory in a completely different way. So just stay with me until the end of this video and you'll learn knowledge that I'm pretty confident you'll struggle to find elsewhere on YouTube. So, first up, let's talk about an important art concept you've probably never heard before, ti, which describes the energy or vibe of colors, but not in a hippie way. While Western artists often obsess over perfect hue matches, Chinese artists tend to care more about capturing the mood and emotion of their subjects using saturation and brightness. But what does that actually mean in practice? Well, instead of trying to decide if blue and orange are complimentary in the offer, Chinese artists ask the most important question of all. What feeling do I want my viewers to feel when looking at my art? They then pick colors accordingly, not just based on hue, contrary to what we've mostly been taught. Instead, they mostly base it on saturation, which matters much more to the mood of a scene than you might expect. For example, think about pastels. You've likely noticed how soft pastel colors often feel calm, comforting, and serene. But have you ever wondered why? It's because lower saturation and higher brightness naturally soothe the viewer. Conversely, colors with high saturation and a lower brightness often feel more powerful, more intense, and often signal drama or tension. This makes sense to our monkey brains because we would rarely ever see such saturated colors out in nature unless it was something important like a ripe fruit or blood. Our brains would stay more alert because of that. And here's the part most people miss. Saturation doesn't just change how bright something feels. It changes how much attention it demands. The human eye is wired to seek out the most saturated point in any composition. So even if your overall scene is perfectly composed, a single overly saturated spot can hijack the viewer's focus entirely. That's why masters use saturation sparingly as a form of a visual hierarchy. They let the calm muted areas do the heavy lifting, then place one or two areas of a richer color exactly where your eyes want to land. Meaning to apply this to your own artworks, you can just throw away all the concepts you've and analogous palettes to build visual intrigue. So rather than strictly sticking to color wheels, ask yourself, is this scene calm or intense? Should it feel gentle or energetic? And adjust the saturation and brightness first instead of playing into the western cliche of red for danger and blue for calm. Then watch your work instantly level up in emotional impact. But let's keep going deeper because the next layer of this concept reveals another hidden gem of Chinese color theory which is sole. This is a gamecher because it completely ignores a rigid color theory rules in favor of storytelling and emotional authenticity. The direct translation doesn't do it justice, so I'll explain what it would involve. Imagine painting a serene river scene in a quiet countryside. Some western trained artists might default to complimentary blues and greens, creating something technically correct. But Chinese artists might do things a bit differently, using whites for the river and choosing softer muted greens, creating a more empty and airy feeling to the painting which immerses the viewer. So instead of thinking of coloring objects in a simplified way of tree okay green water okay blue you can try thinking of what should the water feel like in this scene and this can often mean that you don't even choose blue as the color for the water. So the general idea of futai is that colors should be assigned based on the nature of the subject not just visual balance. This is why you would often see rivers painted in earthy grays rather than the textbook blue or skin tones built with muted pinks and grays rather than high saturation peach. So next time you paint, instead of picking colors based purely on harmony, think what story or emotion am I trying to show? The result might surprise you because the goal isn't accuracy anymore. The simple trick to this is to remove color from your reference entirely. Yep, we're removing the color to paint color. Let me explain. We'll convert it to black and white. Then reimagine the colors from scratch based on emotion rather than what you see. Ask yourself, what temperature fits this emotion? What saturation level supports it? When you start thinking that way, you're not copying the world anymore. You're reinterpreting it. That's the heart of sole futai using color not as description but as expression. Now this last concept is where the real mastery comes in because what most people think of as gray doesn't actually exist in real life. Every gray takes on the qualities of the light and color around it. This means the same gray can appear warm in one context and cold in another. You've probably seen this with a various of famous examples such as this one where the background of the gray makes it look slightly orange or blue even though it's actually the same gray. It's not just about picking the right color. It's about letting the color react to its environment. This is yet another reason why all these realistic and artistic portraits by Chinese artists have a distinct type of just style about them. The colors are simply based on a different concept and objective. Instead of trying to push colors into the portrait like you normally would, you know, choosing orange for something that's orange or blue for something that's blue, the masters will often utilize this concept of to instead use grays to represent a certain color. This way, you're able to have a more harmonious color scheme since the colors are closer together. Think muted lavender and shadow or softer peach in skin tones. So, how can you actually apply this to your own work? Start by thinking in temperature, not hue. When you look at a subject, don't ask, "What color is this?" Instead, ask, "Is this area warm or cool?" Then, pick a desaturated color that fits that temperature. You'll notice that your colors start to react to each other more naturally instead of clashing. Next, stop using neutral gray straight from your palette. Mix your grays from the colors already in the scene. If your painting has a lot of warm tones, let some of that warmth bleed it into your shadows and backgrounds. That shared pigment makes everything feel like it exists under the same light source. You can also use colored grays to control how saturated your painting feels. A painting where every color is bright and intense quickly feels chaotic. But when you surround those vivid areas with subtle colored grays, your eyes finally has space to rest. The saturated spots suddenly feel richer and more powerful without you touching their brightness. But if you want to actually try to incorporate some of the teachings of Chinese artists, then be sure to check out this video here and check out the description for my brushes. Don't forget to like and subscribe if you enjoyed this video.

For that reason, they can signal the importance of ethics and actually improve attitudes and reactions among non-target group members. And then the final thing they can do is they can result in false progress. They can sort of motivate people to take short cuts that make the diversity numbers look better without creating sort of true, underlying change in terms of people's experiences. So, finally in thinking about all these different types of unintended consequences that diversity initiatives might produce. This has some pretty important practical implications for managers and for efforts to try to make these initiatives more effective. So, a really common phenomenon or thing that happens in organizations is that leaders look at just representation. How well are we doing in terms of the number of women and minorities in this organization? And they use that as a still indicator of whether or not a diversity initiative is effective. What this all suggests though is that really, if you wanna understand what diversity initiatives are doing, you need to take a much broader perspective. You need to look at not only things like target group representation, but also things like, well, what are the attitudes like among non-target members? Is it hurting their commitment and their engagement in the organization? You also need to look at things like, well what's happening on a more micro-individual level? What's happening or how's this playing out in the context and sort of everyday hiring and promotion decisions. And then you also need to be really careful about how you think about measuring progress towards diversity goals. Make sure you're measuring in a way that reflects true change, not using metrics that are subject to a false progress effects.

This technique involves painting slightly brighter areas around the darker parts of the face, just like this. It helps give the face a more defined and structured look while also making it appear brighter and more balanced overall. The next step is focusing on the eyes. In this case, the eyes are brown, so you might not notice a huge difference. But if you're working with colored eyes, you can use the hue/saturation tool to adjust the color and paint over the iris. Just make sure the blending mode is set to screen. To take it a step further, create an exposure adjustment layer. Increase the brightness and paint over the bottom part of the eye. And this mimics how light naturally hits the iris, brightening just the lower section. Once that's done, we move on to the mouth. I'll increase the saturation to 100% and paint over the tongue. then reduce it to make it look a natural pink. If it looks good, I might also enhance the lips slightly, but be careful not to overdo it. We don't want them to look like they're wearing lipstick. Remember, you can always adjust the opacity later if the effect feels too strong. The next step is adding selective color. This tool is great for adjusting skin tones and can really make or break your face edits. It honestly deserves a whole separate video. It's especially useful if your image has slightly off colors. For now, just experiment with the sliders, adjusting each color until you achieve the tone you're aiming for. For this tutorial, I'll exaggerate it a bit so the face really pops, similar to Mr. Beast thumbnails. Once that's done, I'll merge all the layers together and go back into the camera raw filter to tweak sharpness and texture, adding more detail. After that, I'll drag and drop a background. It's literally just a random one. I'll reduce its saturation and brightness to make it darker, which sets the stage for the glow effect, the most important part of today's tutorial. To create the glow, I'll select a brush with zero hardness and 50% flow. Then click once or twice behind the subject. I'll change the blending mode to linear dodge. Add. I'll repeat the same step with a pure white brush to make the glow look more like a smooth gradient. Next, I'll duplicate the layer and add a blue inner glow. Then, I'll apply a layer mask and paint only over the areas where it's needed. After that, I'll select the brush again and using a clipping mask, paint over the shoulders to make it look like the light is passing through them. Adjusting the blending mode is always necessary to make the effect look natural. Next, I'll add a curves layer, but instead of adjusting the overall brightness, I'll focus on the color tones. For example, I'll boost the blues and reduce the reds. Using a brush, I'll paint some light reflections over the face. Don't worry if it feels a bit wild at first since you can erase anything later. After that, I'll create two new layers, group them, and set the group's blending mode to linear dodge. Add. I'll fill the bottom layer with pure black and apply a gradient map like this one. You can create your own gradient if you prefer. Then, I'll clip the gradient map to the second layer and continue painting over the face with the brush. This technique might feel a bit strange at first, but with practice, you'll master it. - Why your Netflix thumbnails don't look like mine: Kind: captions Language: en When you’re surfing through Netflix on the bus, the train, work, or in the comfort of your couch at home — how do you pick what to watch? Is it a catchy title? Maybe an interesting synopsis? Perhaps it’s the unwillingness to watch another episode of The Office... “Save Bandit!” [mewling cry of a cat ] Or just maybe, a particular piece of cover art speaks to your spirit? But go on your friend’s Netflix account — if they aren’t still using your subscription — and you may find the cover art there doesn’t interest you. In fact, what you see might be completely different. It's no accident — Netflix's thumbnails are all tailor made... for you. At its heart, Netflix is all about creating personalized experiences — or, rather, calculating them. They’ll draw you in with curated trailers of upcoming releases, point out new episodes from previously watched videos, and even gauge your interest in content via match scores. And while streaming services are notoriously tight-lipped about sharing their viewership data... Over the years, Netflix has shared glimpses into how their technology works. According to internal studies, a typical viewer spends 1.8 seconds considering each title, and Netflix believes it only has 90 seconds to get your attention before you move onto another activity. And among all the things that could catch your attention and make you watch a show– or several— Netflix found that the biggest influence were the thumbnails. Humans are intensely visual creatures. Our eyes move three to four times a second to process new information. And because Netflix’s goal is to get your attention and hold it, the company puts a lot of work into choosing every thumbnail you’ll see. But before they can decide what image will show up on your account, they have to sift through a ton of data. An hour-long Stranger Things episode has almost 86,000 video frames. To figure out which ones will make the best thumbnails, Netflix uses a pretty scientific selection process called Aesthetic Visual Analysis, or AVA. AVA is a set of tools and algorithms that search Netflix videos for the best images and pull them out to create thumbnails. The process can be broken down into two basic steps. First is frame annotation. A program analyzes every static video frame of a video, and image recognition algorithms use information gleaned from each shot to create metadata. The metadata is like an electronic fingerprint — identifying characteristics unique to each video frame. All of this info helps build a database of information that makes it easier to pick out the best images for thumbnails later. And to sort all this data, the company groups it into roughly three categories that are key to identifying good images: Visual — focusing on brightness, color, contrast, and motion blur. Contextual, which documents face and object detection, motion, and shot angles. And compositional — which focuses on visual principles in cinematography, photography, and design. The second step is a process called image ranking. An algorithm uses the metadata to pick out specific shots that Netflix has determined are the most attractive and clickable: ones that aren’t blurry, have varied imagery, feature major characters, and don’t contain sensitive or unauthorized branded content. Then, finally, a creative team steps in to use the best images to design the thumbnail artwork. But the process doesn’t stop there — Netflix still has to figure out which ones work best for each user. A/B testing is executed — again, again, and again. You’ll regularly see changes in your thumbnails — based on your engagement with previous titles. On the most basic level, let’s say you’re a fan of comedy, and you’ve watched a bunch of stand-up specials. When you search for Good Will Hunting, you may get a thumbnail with Robin Williams, a famous comedian, and one of the movie’s main characters. But people more into romance titles could be shown the cover art with the two leads kissing. There are also regional differences. From glancing at a show’s thumbnails across different countries, you could infer Germany is more into abstract images, and US viewers may prefer clearly defined characters and story plots. Though there are a considerable number of thumbnails to choose from, and lots of science that goes into each decision, it doesn’t mean Netflix gets it right all the time. One Twitter user found the cover art for, “Like Father” a movie starring Kristen Bell, Kelsey Grammer, and Seth Rogen, had cover art that didn’t exactly match who the lead actors in the film were. It was also kinda odd to see on my own account, that the Catwoman thumb has an image of a barely recognizable supporting actress Sharon Stone, and Blade II had someone other than its star, Wesley Snipes, in the thumbnail. Netflix is obsessed with A/B testing new features like video promos, intro skipping, and auto-playing trailers — just as obsessively as they are with testing thumbnails. Netflix wants everyone to watch more, so it’s unlikely they’ll stop doing these tests. And if you don’t like being a guinea pig, there is the option to opt out. But with binge-watching quickly becoming a national pastime, it’s likely that, when Netflix asks you, "Are you still watching?" You will be. Hey! "Pay It" helps you reduce your balance by making small payments throughout the month. And "Plan It" can help you split purchases over $100 up over time. You can check it out at americanexpress.com/payitplanit And thanks again to American Express, their support made this series possible.

- The Psychology of Top 0.1% Youtube Thumbnails: Kind: captions Language: en Only the top YouTubers truly understand that&nbsp; getting people to click on your thumbnail is the difference between 10&nbsp; views and 10 million views. So, let's go over the insane psychological&nbsp; tricks that the biggest YouTubers use. I've been obsessing over YouTube&nbsp; thumbnails for over a decade now, popularized some of the most popular&nbsp; thumbnail formats on the platform, and I've worked alongside the&nbsp; biggest creators in the industry and the the biggest. Now, the most important part of your thumbnail&nbsp; without a question is the actual idea. Because if the idea is garbage, well,&nbsp; you can only polish that so much. If your video is something basic&nbsp; like, you went shopping today,&nbsp;&nbsp; you played a game of Fortnite, etc., the thumbnail will naturally be an&nbsp; extension of that and be pretty mediocre. That's why the biggest YouTubers will actually&nbsp; reverse engineer everything from the idea. And once you have that, the thumbnail&nbsp; and title will naturally just be awesome. But of course, there's also many other things to&nbsp; consider that will make or break your thumbnail, like taking into account what&nbsp; is called the curiosity gap. So, for instance, if I showed you something&nbsp; that asked a question, I think this is a great&nbsp;&nbsp; example and it's definitely been used in a lot&nbsp; of case studies, but this video by Veritasium, why is there 96 million black&nbsp; balls on this reservoir? This is his most viewed video on his entire&nbsp; channel, and it illustrates the curiosity gap&nbsp;&nbsp; extremely well. It literally asks the question&nbsp; and then of course the viewer, anyone seeing this&nbsp;&nbsp; sees the absurdity of this goes, why is there that&nbsp; many black balls on this reservoir? And then they&nbsp;&nbsp; click the video to fill in that gap. However, if&nbsp; you give the answer to that gap, which a lot of&nbsp;&nbsp; people do, the gap is closed. You don't want&nbsp; to give the answer away because then there's&nbsp;&nbsp; no reason to click the video. Now, the next thing&nbsp; I consider is the scroll stopping pattern or the&nbsp;&nbsp; interrupt. Basically, how well does your thumbnail&nbsp; stop a viewer scrolling? There's a few good ways&nbsp;&nbsp; to think about this, but one of the things that's&nbsp; really stuck with me throughout my career is the&nbsp;&nbsp; half a second rule. So, literally just pull up&nbsp; your thumbnail and flash it on the screen for&nbsp;&nbsp; half a second. Do you understand what's going on&nbsp; in the thumbnail? If you don't, then it's probably&nbsp;&nbsp; not a good thumbnail. Because when viewers look&nbsp; at thumbnails, they don't sit there and analyze&nbsp;&nbsp; it. They just glance at it. And you do this by&nbsp; having clean composition, a clean idea, and also&nbsp;&nbsp; it should contrast well against the competition,&nbsp; i.e. the purple cow factor that I've talked about&nbsp;&nbsp; in the past. The better your thumbnail and video&nbsp; is at differentiating itself from the competition&nbsp;&nbsp; in a good way, the more it is going to tap into&nbsp; that scroll stopping behavior. Something that&nbsp;&nbsp; will also help with this is understanding color&nbsp; theory. Some of the key pillars of understanding&nbsp;&nbsp; color theory for thumbnails is like things like&nbsp; brights attract. Your eyes naturally scan and go&nbsp;&nbsp; towards the brightest thing on the image. So these&nbsp; are the things that are going to attract attention&nbsp;&nbsp; first. Just think of people like we're moths&nbsp; attracted to the bright part in the image. Next,&nbsp;&nbsp; you want to think about contrasting colors,&nbsp; things that are the opposite of the color or are&nbsp;&nbsp; complimentary colors. So for instance, if you have&nbsp; something that is bright red as a subject in the&nbsp;&nbsp; in the image, well, you don't really want to do a&nbsp; background that's orange or something like that,&nbsp;&nbsp; right? Because it's going to blend in. However,&nbsp; if you do a background that's blue or green,&nbsp;&nbsp; it is going to push your attention towards that&nbsp; contrasting color. Now, you also have to be&nbsp;&nbsp; careful with this because you need to understand&nbsp; why you're doing it and why you're bringing&nbsp;&nbsp; attention to certain uh focal points of the image.&nbsp; If you just start spamming a bunch of contrasting&nbsp;&nbsp; colors, it's going to look like a bunch of&nbsp; nonsense. Another good thing to know about&nbsp;&nbsp; color theory is that the white background usually&nbsp; wins most of the time. This is contextual and it&nbsp;&nbsp; can change in your niche, but most of the time the&nbsp; white background wins because it's just brighter.&nbsp;&nbsp; it brings more attention to your thumbnail.&nbsp; And lastly, on the colors bringing you to a&nbsp;&nbsp; focal point, again, like if you wanted people&nbsp; to look at the object someone's holding and&nbsp;&nbsp; then you put a bunch of bright colors around it,&nbsp; even though you're technically contrasting the&nbsp;&nbsp; colors against that that image or that subject,&nbsp; the focal point isn't going towards that subject&nbsp;&nbsp; because it's drowned out. The first thing that happens is what I call the visual stun gun. Essentially, they switch into a comprehension mode and they're actively trying to figure out what it is that grabbed their attention. So, step one is that visual stun gun. You need to make the thumbnail compelling enough to visually trigger that stun gun effect. And there's actually seven different things you can do in the thumbnail design to give yourself the best chance to create that stun gun reaction. And I'm going to walk through those in a minute. But step one is that visual stun. Now, once the viewer is locked on and they've switched from a passive scrolling to an active comprehension mode, their interest is peaked. So then all they want to do is fully understand what the video could be about and what's in it for them. And here's a critical piece in the psychology flow. Typically, the viewer is not able to gather a full understanding of what the video is about from just the thumbnail alone. It may peak a ton of curiosity, but the image alone will not get them to click. And so, this is where step two happens, where they shift their attention from the image down to the title. And they do this because words are easier to concretely understand than images. Images give us more data, but they're often up to interpretation. Words are much clearer and more specific. So, in step two, the viewer then reads the title to get a more direct sense of what the video is going to be about. And I call step two title value hunting. The viewer is essentially looking at the title to understand if they should opt into watching because it's going to offer some value for them. This is why the title and thumbnail together are often referred to as YouTube packaging. You really can't win without optimizing for both and the viewer consumes both at the same time. Now, I'll explain in a minute how to optimize the clarity and clickability of the title, but just to reframe where we're at so far in the psychology flow. So far, the viewer started paying attention from the visual stun gun and then gut check the relevance of the video for them in the title value hunting. Now, here is where things get interesting. After value hunting the title, they still won't click because step three is when the viewer goes back up to the thumbnail to more deeply comprehend what's in it. And this is called visual validation. Now that the viewer has a firmer grasp of the topic and the promise made in the title, they can anchor when visually trying to comprehend what's going on in the thumbnail. If the thumbnail does a good job of supporting the value promised by the title, and the viewer wants that value, they're going to click. So, the psychology flow is thumbnail to title back to thumbnail. That's how a viewer consumes the information and decides to click. It's visual stun gun to title value hunting, back to visual validation. And understanding this flow is so important because it explains why certain YouTube packaging works better than others. If you have a thumbnail design that's easy to understand, but it doesn't pop visually, then you'll never pass the visual stun gun phase. If you have a thumbnail that visually grabs attention, but the title promise is weak, then it's going to get somebody to look at it, but they won't click because the promise isn't compelling. If you have a strong title and a visually interesting image, but the elements in the thumbnail themselves don't support that title promise, then the viewer is not going to click because they'll be confused. Director&nbsp; George Miller took a bold approach, flooding the&nbsp;&nbsp; desert apocalypse with high-contrast orange and&nbsp; teal—hot, searing, and surreal. The extreme color&nbsp;&nbsp; palette heightens the chaos and amplifies the&nbsp; sensation of heat, adrenaline, and desperation. So before you even pick up&nbsp; the camera, ask yourself:&nbsp;&nbsp; What do I want my audience to feel in this&nbsp; moment? Because color—used intentionally—is&nbsp;&nbsp; your secret weapon to make them feel&nbsp; it… long before they understand why. Every color triggers a psychological&nbsp; response—and filmmakers can use this to&nbsp;&nbsp; shape the emotional DNA of a scene. Let’s explore&nbsp; how color taps directly into the human psyche,&nbsp;&nbsp; and how you can use it intentionally to&nbsp; control mood, tone, and character perception. Blue is one of the most versatile emotional&nbsp; colors in filmmaking. It can evoke serenity,&nbsp;&nbsp; like the expansive, contemplative skies&nbsp; in 'The Tree of Life', where blue brings&nbsp;&nbsp; spiritual reflection and cosmic peace. But&nbsp; blue can also suggest emotional distance or&nbsp;&nbsp; cold logic. In 'The Imitation Game', for&nbsp; instance, the cold blue hues surrounding&nbsp;&nbsp; Alan Turing highlight his isolation and&nbsp; emotional disconnect, even amid brilliance. Use blue when you want to convey&nbsp; stillness, silence, loneliness,&nbsp;&nbsp; intellectual distance, or&nbsp; a quiet sense of longing. Red is emotionally intense—it elevates the&nbsp; viewer’s pulse and commands attention. It&nbsp;&nbsp; doesn’t whisper—it screams.&nbsp; In 'Inglourious Basterds',&nbsp;&nbsp; red is used not just for visual&nbsp; flair, but as a storytelling weapon. During the climactic Nazi movie&nbsp; premiere, Shosanna wears a bold,&nbsp;&nbsp; fiery red gown—standing out as the&nbsp; only woman in red amid a sea of grays,&nbsp;&nbsp; blacks, and military uniforms. That dress is a&nbsp; declaration. It radiates confidence, defiance,&nbsp;&nbsp; and vengeance. It tells us—without dialogue—that&nbsp; she holds the power in that room. As the reel&nbsp;&nbsp; rolls and her plan unfolds, the red becomes a&nbsp; symbol of blood, justice, and fury unleashed. Use red to ignite passion, provoke urgency,&nbsp;&nbsp; symbolize control or power—or to&nbsp; foreshadow destruction and rebellion. Green is a dual-natured color in&nbsp; cinema. It can symbolize growth,&nbsp;&nbsp; harmony, and rebirth—but with a shift in hue, it&nbsp; easily becomes alien, obsessive, or unsettling. In 'Vertigo', Hitchcock uses green with&nbsp; psychological precision. When Madeleine reappears&nbsp;&nbsp; as Judy, she's bathed in an eerie green glow from&nbsp; a neon hotel sign. It’s not just atmospheric—it’s&nbsp;&nbsp; a visual cue of resurrection and obsession,&nbsp; a ghostly return from the past. The unnatural&nbsp;&nbsp; tint communicates that something is wrong,&nbsp; blurring the line between reality and illusion. Green becomes a haunting presence,&nbsp;&nbsp; signaling emotional instability and the&nbsp; protagonist’s descent into delusion. Use green to balance themes of renewal&nbsp; with unease, or to visualize environments&nbsp;&nbsp; that feel otherworldly, psychologically&nbsp; charged, or morally ambiguous. Even the&nbsp;&nbsp; difference between a soft sage and a neon&nbsp; green can completely alter emotional tone. Yellow is one of the most psychologically&nbsp; ambiguous colors in film. It radiates warmth,&nbsp;&nbsp; sunshine, and nostalgia—but push it too far, and&nbsp; it tips into unease, instability, or even madness. In 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood', yellow is&nbsp; everywhere—from Cliff Booth’s mustard shirt to&nbsp;&nbsp; the warm California lighting. It evokes&nbsp; the golden glow of late '60s Hollywood,&nbsp;&nbsp; creating a sun-drenched world of faded&nbsp; dreams and youthful energy. But it also&nbsp;&nbsp; masks the underlying tension. The same golden&nbsp; haze begins to feel surreal, like a memory&nbsp;&nbsp; that's too perfect to trust—especially as&nbsp; the film inches toward its violent climax. Use soft yellows for a nostalgic, dreamlike&nbsp; tone—but crank up the saturation to slip into&nbsp;&nbsp; discomfort, mania, or psychological chaos. Yellow&nbsp; walks a fine line between warmth and warning. Purple is a rare but powerful cinematic&nbsp; color—often reserved for moments of&nbsp;&nbsp; spiritual significance, royal lineage,&nbsp; and emotional depth. It’s the color of&nbsp;&nbsp; mystery and transformation, sitting between&nbsp; the calm of blue and the energy of red.&nbsp; In 'Black Panther', purple is used with incredible&nbsp; intention. It appears in the ancestral plane,&nbsp;&nbsp; where T’Challa meets the kings who came&nbsp; before him. The sky glows with soft, surreal&nbsp;&nbsp; purples—conveying otherworldliness, reverence,&nbsp; and ancestral wisdom. This hue becomes a visual&nbsp;&nbsp; signature for Wakanda’s regal heritage and its&nbsp; spiritual connection to legacy and identity. You’ll also see it woven into the heart-shaped&nbsp; herb ceremony, where purple energy pulses through&nbsp;&nbsp; T’Challa’s body—symbolizing both power transfer&nbsp; and spiritual elevation. The filmmakers didn’t&nbsp;&nbsp; choose purple by accident—it’s the bridge&nbsp; between the physical and the metaphysical. Use purple when you want to signal royalty,&nbsp;&nbsp; deep inner transformation, or&nbsp; connection to a higher purpose. Orange brings energy and warmth,&nbsp; but also intensity. In 'Mad Max:&nbsp;&nbsp; Fury Road', orange skies and dust dominate&nbsp; the color palette, evoking extreme heat,&nbsp;&nbsp; urgency, and desperation.&nbsp; It’s energetic and visceral. Use it to bring boldness&nbsp; and adrenaline to a scene. Black and white aren’t just about&nbsp; absence or presence of color—they’re&nbsp;&nbsp; emotional and symbolic anchors. Black evokes finality, grief,&nbsp;&nbsp; fear, or moral ambiguity. White represents purity,&nbsp;&nbsp; truth, or even emptiness, depending on context. In 'The Batman', director Matt Reeves&nbsp; and cinematographer Greig Fraser&nbsp;&nbsp; masterfully lean into a monochromatic visual&nbsp; language—bathed in deep shadows, muted tones,&nbsp;&nbsp; and sharp contrasts. Gotham itself is&nbsp; cloaked in black: rain-soaked streets,&nbsp;&nbsp; dim alleyways, and cavernous spaces reflect&nbsp; a world drowning in corruption and fear. Batman—literally the man in black—is not just&nbsp; hiding in the shadows, he is the shadow. His&nbsp;&nbsp; moral journey is painted in tones of darkness,&nbsp; as he confronts what justice really means in a&nbsp;&nbsp; decaying city. Even light, when it appears,&nbsp; is often harsh or cold—white headlights,&nbsp;&nbsp; flickering fluorescents, or brief flashes&nbsp; of truth in a world steeped in lies. This careful balance of black and white&nbsp; deepens the story’s moral complexity and&nbsp;&nbsp; mirrors Batman’s internal struggle: Vengeance vs.&nbsp; Hope. Fear vs. Justice. Isolation vs. Redemption. Use black and white tones to strip your&nbsp; story to its moral core—revealing truth,&nbsp;&nbsp; loss, or existential weight beneath the surface. Don’t just think of color as a background&nbsp; layer—treat it like a character. It should&nbsp;&nbsp; evolve with the story, reflect emotion&nbsp; arcs, and even foreshadow what’s to come.” Now that you understand how colors&nbsp; affect emotions and storytelling—how&nbsp;&nbsp; do you actually plan your color choices like&nbsp; a pro? - How Do Light Colors Impact Audience Perception In Media Production? - Media Jobs: Kind: captions Language: en [Music] How do light colors impact audience perception in media production? Imagine walking into a room bathed in bright red lights or a scene glowing with cool blue hues. The colors you see in media are more than just visuals. They shape how you feel and what you think. When media professionals work with lighting, they use color choices to tell stories and guide emotions. This is a key part of technical production skills and understanding lighting techniques. Warm colors like red, orange, and yellow are often used to create energy, excitement, or passion. Think about a concert or a sports event where these colors make you feel hyped up. Bright, saturated, warm colors grab attention and make scenes feel lively. On the other hand, cool colors such as blue, green, and purple tend to produce calmness, serenity, or mystery. These are great for scenes that want to feel reflective or futuristic. The intensity of the color also matters. Bright, vivid colors make scenes feel more dynamic, and engaging. Muted or desaturated tones can make a scene seem more serious, nostalgic, or tense. For example, a romantic scene might use warm, soft lighting to create intimacy, while a horror scene might use cold, desaturated tones to build tension. Lighting tools like colored gels, lead fixtures, and spotlights help control these colors precisely. Using these tools, media creators can highlight specific parts of a scene or direct viewers focus. For example, a spotlight with a red gel can make a character appear more intense or aggressive. Proper placement and color choice can guide viewers eyes exactly where the creator wants them to look. Color grading in post-prouction is another way to influence perception. Filmmakers adjust colors after filming to support the story's mood. For instance, horror movies often use blue green tones to create an ease, while romantic films might add warm golden hues for softness. These choices change how viewers feel about what they see on screen. Developing skills in lighting and color is essential for media professionals. Knowing how to select and mix colors, program lighting systems, and collaborate with directors helps create the right mood. Understanding the technical differences between formats like RAW, log, and Rex 7009 is also important for maintaining color consistency. Colors can even affect how people physically respond. Certain wavelengths can make viewers feel alert or relaxed. For example, blue light can be calming, but too much can disrupt sleep if used late at night. This is important for productions with long hours where crew and talent need to stay alert and comfortable. In short, light colors are a powerful tool in media production. They influence emotions, focus attention, and shape the viewer's experience. Mastering lighting techniques and understanding color theory helps media professionals craft content that connects with audiences and tells stories more effectively. Developing these skills is a key step in building a successful career in the industry.

- Color Psychology - How Colors Influence Your Choices and Feelings: Kind: captions Language: en Brainy Dose Presents: Color Psychology – How Colors Influence Your Choices and Feelings Although we don’t often think about it, colors have a significant impact on people. It may not be the biggest surprise, but the color of food can affect how it tastes, the color of a room can affect how you feel, the color of your clothes can affect how attractive members of the opposite gender find you - and so on. Color psychology is the study of how color affects different individuals and their actions. But before we dive any further, there’s one really important factor to consider, and that is culture. The culture in which an individual is raised in can influence how they react to color - suggesting that reactions to colors can be somewhat learned. A particular color may be a sign of good luck in one culture, but a sign of bad luck in another. In a case like this, the color is going to affect the mood of each person in different ways. Colors play an important role in our lives, and they are an interesting piece to a puzzle of different things that influence our moods in everyday situations. With that in mind, here are a few interesting ways in which color can affect you. Number One - Colors Can Be Stimulating Or Calming When it comes to colors, their effects can vary based on whether they are considered warm or cool. These terms are often used in art classes, but they offer unique insight into how color can affect a person. Of course, these statements can vary between different colors, but for the most part, there are some things in common. Warm colors are brighter - like yellow, orange, or red. These colors can encourage stimulation - but are sufficient in small or limited amounts. Seeing too much of a warm color can become irritating or annoying. If you ever find yourself feeling tired, exhausted, or as if you’re missing a sort of spark in life, a reasonable insertion of warm colors may be the key to subconsciously brighten up your mood. When it comes to cool colors, they tend to be more popular when someone is looking for a peaceful and calming effect in their everyday life. Shades of blue and green are considered to be most restful, calming, or relaxing. The color blue represents the sky and sea - and these are the elements that naturally make us calm. This makes it ideal for places where you may want to meditate, rest, or rid yourself from the stressful events you may have encountered throughout your day. Blue is a very powerful color that helps encourage relaxation - making it a very good choice for bedrooms. The color green has similar properties - as it symbolizes nature and serenity. There’s even some science behind green’s calming effect - research has been able to show that there is less effort needed to see the color green - thus, the muscles in the eyes don’t have to work as hard. Purple on the other hand, is a cool color that is most widely used to encourage creative energy and charge. It’s a mixture of red and blue, which gives it sparks of relaxation and peace - but also encouragement and potential stimulation. Number Two - Color Can Mean Different Things It’s literally IMPOSSIBLE to narrow one color down to a solid meaning - and the reason for this is mainly cultural. Most colors have multiple symbolic or cultural meanings, even if you choose to ignore the fact that certain colors will influence certain emotions or memories. Take the color black as an example. When people think about the color black, they often think of mystery, death, evil, or emptiness. But the color black can also be interpreted to represent elegance or formality - such as a nice tuxedo or a sleek dress. None of these things are wrong, in fact, they are just some of the different things that the color itself can symbolize. Take red as another example. Some people think of the color red as representing power, aggression, strength, or danger. But other individuals may look at the color red and immediately think of love, lust, passion and desire. It would be easy to argue that the two different meanings are on opposite sides of the symbolic spectrum. However, in many Western cultures, the color red represents all of these things. This makes interpreting how color affects mood somewhat challenging, because what people see in the same color can be drastically different things. Number Three - Colors Can Determine Buying Choices Color Psychology is used widely by various marketing agencies, grocery stores, designers, etc. - and it’s definitely working for them. For instance, research has shown that products or packaging with red labels will grab your attention faster. Red is an inviting color to look at - and it works best with impulsive shoppers. The color orange is mostly associated with fairness or affordability. You may find that stores offering good value will use orange to reflect their fair prices. Green is most often used to attract individuals who are more eco-friendly. While white is a color that implies purity - which is why most skin care companies will package their top skin care brands in white. Purple portrays royalty or luxury, and it is also used often in the beauty industry - especially when it comes to anti-aging products. A purple box persuades people into paying a higher price - by making them think that the product has special properties. Black is another color that’s used often - due to its portrayal of quality or sophistication. This color is most often used with high-end products, but can make cheaper items seem more valuable as well. Number Four - Colors Can Make You More Confident And Attractive Black and red have been found to be the staple colors of beauty and fashion across the world. They have also been voted as the colors which inspire the most confidence. Men and women both prefer wearing black to interviews or gatherings of importance - because black gives them a boost of confidence. When it comes to first dates specifically, women would rather wear something red - as it makes them feel sexier. While men will typically choose to wear something black or blue. Interestingly, not only do men like wearing black or blue to impress women, women actually prefer those two colors the most on men as well. Number Five - Color Can Make You Eat Less Or More Aside from affecting your mood, color can also affect your appetite. In fact, the color of your kitchen walls or dining wear can affect how much you eat! Research has shown that individuals who eat off of red plates are found to eat less food. White plates on the other hand, seem bigger than they really are - therefore, they encourage you to eat more. The colors yellow and orange are also thought to influence appetite by increasing your hunger. So if you’re looking to lose a few extra pounds, consider changing up the scenery in your kitchen. Number Six - Colors Can Match With Scent It is possible for certain colors to match scents - but only in a limited or personal way. This is strange to think about as they play on various senses, since we can’t see scent or smell color. However, there are many colors and scents that blend well together. One great example of how this works is the color green. Maybe you love the scent of pine. If you want to enhance your experience with that scent, you could do ‘essential oil’ aromatherapy, in a room painted green. Of course, the way these combinations enhance mood will vary from person to person, but it’s certainly worth a try. Number Seven - Colors Can Encourage Feelings Of Happiness Certain colors tend to naturally encourage happiness more often than not. These are not strict rules when it comes to the effects of color though, so think of them more like guidelines. With that said, when it comes to colors that can naturally encourage happiness, blue is actually at the top of the list. There is no other color that seems to get such universal love across gender and cultural lines. So it shouldn’t be surprising that blue is a potentially happy color! Green has been found to be the second favorite color among men - and the third among women. Yellow is another color that encourages happiness - hence the easy association with yellow is the classic smiley face. However, this color is best used in small amounts, as large amounts of yellow can be too bright. The most peculiar choice of color for representing happy feelings is purple. Purple is actually the second most favorite color among women - and is found to be a strong competitor when encouraging happiness. When it comes to men however, purple is the second most hated color. Therefore, there seems to be a gender-biased reaction to certain colors in many cases. Now, going with a favorite color isn’t necessarily a bad idea. But, keep in mind that many colors can be stimulating in nature - and just because someone has a favorite color, it doesn’t mean that the color has the ability to calm them or encourage positive feelings. For instance, many people love the color black, but do not find it to be inspiring or relaxing in any way. Number Eight - Colors Can Incite Unhappiness Just as there are colors that can encourage calmness or happiness in a person, there are colors that do the exact opposite. While having a favorite color does not necessarily mean that color will always play a role in helping you feel better, the opposite may actually be true when it comes to colors you don’t like and their effect on your mood. If you dislike a certain color, chances are that it will do very little to make you happy - in fact, it can easily make you unhappy. Nevertheless, when it comes to hated colors, there are two that seem to stick out the most: Brown is the least popular color among men - and the second least favorite among women. Interestingly, brown happens to represent laziness, filth, or ugliness. It may seem bland and outdated. It’s no surprise that brown doesn’t seem to register with either gender as a favorite! While the color orange represents extravagance and uniqueness, it is the second most hated color. It’s the least popular color among women, and is tied with purple as the second least favorite among men. Although there may be individuals from each gender who prefer one over the other, brown and orange are very clearly the least popular colors of the color spectrum. All in all, colors really do “color” our lives - whether by impacting what we’re subconsciously drawn to, how we express ourselves individually, or how they affect our moods. Since everybody is different, not everyone will react to colors the same way, because colors influence each of us individually on different levels. In addition, there are various general ‘social or cultural’ influences on how color affects us. In this lesson, we show you how&nbsp; to find and use color combinations&nbsp;&nbsp; to make your design effective and colorful. The most basic colors are red, yellow, and, blue. The color wheel is a useful tool. With just&nbsp; one look, we can see every color imaginable. The wheel also helps us to find&nbsp; color combinations like these. With complementary colors, opposites attract.&nbsp; These are two colors that live&nbsp; on opposite sides of the wheel. Some examples of complementary color combinations&nbsp;&nbsp; are green and red, yellow&nbsp; and purple, orange and blue. Because complementary colors are&nbsp; opposites, they have high contrasts.&nbsp; So we use these pairings to stand out. When we talk about how bright or dark a&nbsp; color is, we're talking about its tone.&nbsp; In monochromatic color combinations, we have&nbsp; variations of the same color like these. We get tones, tints, or shades by&nbsp; adding black or white to colors. Monochromatic colors have low contrast. So we use these to give&nbsp; designs a different feeling. What feeling does this design show? Analogous or sometimes called sympathetic colors&nbsp;&nbsp; are colors that sit closely&nbsp; together on the color wheel. Think of these colors as&nbsp; sets that hug one another. These colors match well with some contrast. They make design elements&nbsp; feel related to each other.&nbsp; Like this example. These are just color wheel combinations. We can color pick these or&nbsp; use some handy Canva features.&nbsp; We'll show you how shortly.&nbsp; Once you've landed on a color palette, take a step back to evaluate your design. Does the selection of colors represent&nbsp; the message or feeling you're sending? Use bright yellows to spread positivity or&nbsp; blues to share calm like these examples. Designs are either digital, on&nbsp; screen, or printed like on paper.&nbsp; We publish with colors in these ways. This format is the color mode used for printing.&nbsp; It's also important to keep colors accessible. This helps people see your design.
